title: Rethinking AI Chips: How VSORA Redesigned the Hardware That Runs AI - Semiwiki
gist: VSORA, founded in 2015 by the DiBcom mobile-TV DSP team, argues its reconfigurable DSP architecture already covered roughly 90% of what an AI chip needs, letting it skip the CUDA-defended training market and target inference and the memory wall instead. Its 5nm, 2.5D co-packaged Jotunn8 — 3.2 petaFLOPS FP8, 288GB of fast memory, taped out October 2025 with GUC and TSMC, silicon back May 2026 — is claimed to keep math circuits busy more than 50% of the time versus 10% or less for conventional GPUs on memory-bound work, at under half the power; the author is a VSORA business development executive.

themes.theme: DSP heritage as an unearned AI head start

insights.claim: VSORA's founders spent about a decade at DiBcom building mobile-TV chips and, when two large German automakers demanded a single chip configurable for all global broadcast standards, built their own DSP with roughly 100 operation types executable in a single clock tick because no off-the-shelf part was flexible or powerful enough.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Architectural pedigree from a shipped, hard reconfigurable design is a diligence differentiator versus AI-chip startups building from a clean sheet.
insights.locator: Its founders spent about a decade at a company called DiBcom

insights.claim: When VSORA's team assessed what an AI chip requires, they found they had already built roughly 90 percent of it: dense grids of multiply-and-add circuits, the ability to move large amounts of data at once, and the internal plumbing to keep both fed.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: If true, VSORA's development risk and time-to-silicon are lower than typical startup assumptions, which changes the capital needed to reach production.
insights.quote: They took stock of what an AI chip would require, and found they had already built roughly 90 percent of it
insights.locator: VSORA's DSP Already Covered Roughly 90%

insights.claim: The core AI datapath — a grid of circuits repeatedly multiplying two numbers and adding to a running total in lockstep — is powerful but repetitive and predictable, and therefore an easier engineering problem than a flexible reconfigurable DSP doing many different coordinated things at once.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI-silicon moat away from the MAC array and toward control, scheduling and data routing, where incumbency and experience matter more.
insights.quote: Having solved the harder problem first, the team realized an efficient AI chip wasn’t a leap into something new.
insights.locator: The direction of that overlap is the crucial point

insights.claim: DiBcom's single-chip multi-standard program required 14 tape-outs across digital and RF designs, an experience that led the team to adopt two principles: design for the long haul and build on open, widely shared software foundations.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: The open-software principle is what produced the LLVM-based compiler strategy, the main hedge against CUDA lock-in.
insights.locator: It was, by the team's own admission, a “nightmare,”

insights.claim: VSORA was incorporated in 2015 to build an advanced DSP using LLVM as the backbone compiler, released its IP in 2017, and was pushed toward machine learning by automotive partners in 2018/2019 — meaning its AI pivot was customer-pulled rather than founder-anticipated.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: A decade of pre-AI architecture work explains why a European startup can field data-center-class silicon without hyperscaler-scale funding.
insights.locator: In 2015, the core team of DiBcom regrouped

insights.claim: Training is the phase where Nvidia's CUDA toolset gives it a nearly unbreakable hold on customers, so VSORA deliberately skipped the training fight and targeted inference instead.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Inference-only positioning is the standard challenger playbook; evaluate challengers on whether they concede training explicitly rather than claiming both.
insights.quote: it’s the phase where Nvidia’s software, specifically, a toolset called CUDA that nearly all AI programs are written for, gives it a nearly unbreakable hold on customers
insights.locator: The strategy that followed is worth understanding

insights.claim: Inference runs constantly, 24/7, at massive scale, and is where the real day-to-day cost of running AI is decided, making it the larger recurring-revenue pool even though training gets the attention.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Opex-driven inference economics favor whoever wins on cost per token, a different competitive basis than training-cluster share.
insights.locator: Inference is what happens every time you actually use

insights.claim: VSORA's deployment path exports an existing model from a familiar framework such as PyTorch to ONNX and runs it through an LLVM-based proprietary compiler that generates hardware-specific code, eliminating the need to hand-write the low-level GPU kernels CUDA requires.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Porting friction is the usual reason alternative accelerators fail; a working ONNX-to-LLVM path is the single most important thing to verify in diligence.
insights.locator: Just as important for deployment, the VSORA software stack

insights.claim: The standard AI-hardware startup failure pattern is that building the math circuits was never the hard part — the hard parts are the software everyone already uses and moving data fast enough to keep those circuits busy.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Two-factor screen for any accelerator investment: existing-framework compatibility and achieved memory bandwidth utilization, not peak FLOPS.
insights.quote: The difficult part was never building the circuits that do the math. The difficult part was everything around them
insights.locator: There's a version of the AI hardware story

insights.claim: The memory wall means a modern AI chip can do math far faster than it can be fed data, so expensive math circuits spend most of their time idle waiting for model data to arrive from memory.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Idle silicon is the largest hidden cost in inference fleets; memory bandwidth and packaging, not FLOPS, set real throughput.
insights.locator: And it aimed at the single biggest bottleneck

insights.claim: VSORA claims Jotunn8 keeps its math circuits usefully busy more than 50 percent of the time on real workloads, while conventional GPUs often deliver 10 percent or less of rated peak on the same memory-bound work.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: A 5x utilization delta, if independently confirmed, would matter far more to inference cost per token than peak-FLOPS comparisons.
insights.quote: Conventional GPUs, by comparison, often deliver 10 percent or less of their rated peak on the same memory-bound work
insights.locator: The payoff shows up in efficiency

insights.claim: VSORA's stated design priority was not the headline peak speed number on a spec sheet but the fraction of rated speed delivered on real work, an explicit rejection of benchmark-driven positioning.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Use achieved-versus-peak ratios as the comparison metric when evaluating any inference accelerator claim.
insights.quote: It was the number that actually matters: how much of that rated speed the chip delivers on real work.
insights.locator: VSORA's priority wasn't the big headline speed number

insights.claim: VSORA reports achieving its inference performance at less than half the power of leading GPUs running inference, framing power as a primary competitive axis.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Power-constrained data centers can monetize a 2x efficiency edge directly as additional deployable capacity per megawatt.
insights.quote: VSORA reports doing it on less than half the power versus leading GPUs running inference
insights.locator: And VSORA reports doing it on less than half the power

themes.theme: Jotunn8 silicon status and supply chain

insights.claim: Jotunn8 is built on a 5-nanometer process with processor and memory co-packaged in a single 2.5D chiplet module, rated at 3.2 petaFLOPS in FP8 with 288 gigabytes of fast memory.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: 288GB of co-packaged memory targets large-model inference where capacity, not compute, gates deployment.
insights.locator: VSORA's Jotunn8: From Design to Silicon

insights.claim: Jotunn8 was sent to the factory in October 2025 in partnership with GUC and TSMC, with first physical chips returning in May 2026 and performance characterization currently underway.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Silicon exists but is not yet characterized, so performance claims remain unvalidated; watch for third-party benchmark data as the de-risking event.
insights.locator: The design was sent to the factory in October 2025

insights.claim: A funding round in July 2026 led by Ardian alongside Otium, the European Innovation Council Fund and other new and existing backers is financing the push to get Jotunn8 into customers' hands.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: European sovereign-adjacent capital is funding AI inference silicon, a policy-supported niche distinct from U.S. venture flows.
insights.locator: A funding round in July 2026, led by the investment firm Ardian

insights.claim: VSORA claims to be the only European player capable of the highest tier of data-center AI inference, a sovereignty positioning as much as a technical one.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: European digital-sovereignty procurement could provide a protected first market independent of pure price-performance competition.
insights.quote: makes it the only European player at that level, according to VSORA
insights.locator: That result puts VSORA among a small group

themes.theme: Caveats and how the bet resolves

insights.claim: The author of this account is a business development executive at VSORA, so the utilization, power and tier-leadership claims are company-sourced rather than independently measured.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Discount all comparative claims accordingly and require third-party inference benchmarks before underwriting the thesis.
insights.quote: Lauro Rizzatti is a business development executive at VSORA
insights.locator: Lauro Rizzatti is a business development executive

insights.claim: Whether the design wins will be settled in real data-center racks over the coming year, making the next twelve months the decisive validation window for VSORA's architecture.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Concrete timeline to falsification: absence of named production deployments within a year is itself a negative signal.
insights.quote: Whether the design wins in practice will be settled where these things always are: in the racks of real data centers, over the coming year.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: The underlying wager is on plain economics — whether AI can keep growing without its costs spiraling out of control — rather than on outperforming Nvidia on raw capability.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: If inference cost per token becomes the binding constraint on AI deployment, efficiency-first architectures gain share regardless of peak performance leadership.
insights.locator: A veteran team took a deep expertise
